hints: Think about which classic test uses alkaline aqueous iodine and gives a yellow solid when a methyl carbonyl group is present.
walkthrough:
Link yellow precipitate to a named test**
You have a carbonyl compound plus alkaline aqueous iodine giving a yellow precipitate. That is the signature of the iodoform test, which is positive for methyl ketones of the form $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CO}-$ and for ethanal.
Final answer: triiodomethane / iodoform, $\text{CHI}_{3}$

hints: Look at the formula $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and decide whether the C=O is in the middle of the chain or at the end.
walkthrough:
Name the carbonyl compound**
$\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ has four carbons with the C=O carbon bonded to two other carbons, so it is a ketone. Numbering gives the carbonyl at carbon 2, so the name is butanone, also acceptable as butan-2-one.

hints: Count the atoms in W to get the molecular formula, then remember that aldehydes and ketones with the same formula are functional group isomers.
Keep the same $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$ count but move the C=O to the end of the chain, then branch the carbon skeleton once.
walkthrough:
Work out what must stay the same**
W is $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$. Your isomers must also be $\text{C}_{4}\text{H}_{8}\text{O}$ and must still contain C=O, so think of aldehydes, where CHO is at the end of the chain.

Draw the straight chain and branched aldehydes**
First draw the unbranched chain: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$. Then draw the only branched $\text{C}_{4}$ skeleton with an aldehyde group: $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCHO}$. These are the two aldehyde structural isomers of butanone.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{2}\text{CHO}$ (butanal) and $(\text{CH}_{3})_{2}\text{CHCHO}$ (2-methylpropanal)

hints: Compare $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ with $\text{CH}_{3}\text{CH(OH)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ and check whether oxygen is lost or hydrogen is gained at the carbonyl carbon.
walkthrough:
Spot gain of hydrogen**
The C=O in the ketone becomes CH-OH in the product. Hydrogen has been added across the double bond and no oxygen is removed as such, but gain of hydrogen is reduction in organic chemistry. So reaction 1 is reduction.

hints: Recall the standard mild hydride reagent used at AS level to reduce aldehydes and ketones to alcohols without needing dry conditions.
walkthrough:
Choose the hydride donor**
Ketone to secondary alcohol needs a source of hydride, $\text{H}^{-}$. At AS level the routine reagent is $\text{NaBH}_{4}$, sodium borohydride. $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ also works and is accepted.
Final answer: $\text{NaBH}_{4}$ / sodium borohydride OR $\text{LiAlH}_{4}$ / lithium aluminium hydride

hints: Start by identifying the nucleophile and the electrophilic carbon, remembering where the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks.
Recall how the C=O bond is polarised and which way the curly arrow moves from the double bond.
Think about what charge the oxygen carries after it gains both electrons from the C=O pi bond.
Consider how that negatively charged oxygen is then converted into the OH group in X.
walkthrough:
Set up the first attack**
Picture $\text{CN}^{-}$ with its lone pair on carbon. That carbon is the nucleophile. The carbonyl carbon in $\text{CH}_{3}\text{COCH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ is $\delta+$ because oxygen pulls electrons away, so show $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow from the lone pair on $\text{CN}^{-}$ to the carbonyl carbon.

Break the pi bond correctly**
As the new C-C bond forms, the C=O pi electrons cannot stay there. Draw a second curly arrow starting in the middle of the C=O double bond and pointing onto the oxygen. This gives the tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(O}^{-})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$.

Draw the intermediate carefully**
Show the central carbon bonded to $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CN}$ and $\text{O}^{-}$. The oxygen must carry a full negative charge and two lone pairs plus the single bond, making the intermediate an anion.

Protonate to finish**
The $\text{O}^{-}$ is strongly basic. Draw a curly arrow from a lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ to $\text{H}^{+}$ supplied by HCN. That forms the O-H bond of the cyanohydrin X, $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(OH)(CN)CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, and regenerates $\text{CN}^{-}$.

Final answer: Nucleophilic addition: lone pair on C of $\text{CN}^{-}$ attacks carbonyl C; $\text{C}^{\delta+}-\text{O}^{\delta-}$ dipole shown with curly arrow $\text{C=O}$ to O to give $\text{CH}_{3}\text{C(O}^{-})(\text{CN})\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ intermediate; lone pair on $\text{O}^{-}$ attacks $\text{H}^{+}$ (from HCN) to give X.

hints: Remember the name for stereoisomerism that arises when a molecule can exist as two non-superimposable mirror images.
walkthrough:
Name the stereoisomerism**
X is formed as a pair of mirror image forms that rotate plane polarised light in opposite directions. That type is optical isomerism.
Final answer: optical (isomerism)

hints: Examine the central carbon in X and list its four attached groups to see if any are repeated.
Recall the test for optical activity in terms of how the two mirror images fit on top of each other.
walkthrough:
Prove the carbon is chiral**
Look at the carbon bearing OH and CN in X. It is attached to $\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, OH and CN, four completely different groups. That makes it a chiral centre, also called an asymmetric carbon.

Explain the consequence**
Because of that chiral centre, the molecule can exist in two mirror image forms. Try to overlay them in your mind and the $\text{CH}_{3}$ and $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$ groups swap over, so they are non-superimposable. That pair is a pair of optical isomers, enantiomers.
Final answer: X has a chiral centre / asymmetric carbon atom bonded to four different groups ($\text{CH}_{3}$, $\text{CH}_{2}\text{CH}_{3}$, OH, CN); the two mirror images are non-superimposable.

hints: Start by converting each percentage into moles by dividing by the $A_{r}$: C/12.0, H/1.0, N/14.0, O/16.0.
Then divide all four mole values by the smallest one to get the simplest whole number ratio.
walkthrough:
Convert percent to moles**
Treat percentages as grams in 100 g. Divide by $A_{r}$:
$$\frac{51.3}{12.0} = 4.28 \text{ for C}$$
$$\frac{9.40}{1.0} = 9.40 \text{ for H}$$
$$\frac{12.0}{14.0} = 0.857 \text{ for N}$$
$$\frac{27.3}{16.0} = 1.71 \text{ for O}$$

Simplify to the smallest ratio**
Divide each by the smallest, 0.857:
$$\text{C}: 4.28/0.857 = 4.99$$
$$\text{H}: 9.40/0.857 = 10.97$$
$$\text{N}: 0.857/0.857 = 1$$
$$\text{O}: 1.71/0.857 = 2.00$$
That rounds cleanly to $5:11:1:2$, proving the empirical formula $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{2}$.

hints: Calculate the mass of $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{2}$ and compare it with the given $M_{r}$ of 117.
walkthrough:
Check empirical mass against $M_{r}$**
Add up the empirical mass:
$$M = 5(12.0)+11(1.0)+14.0+2(16.0) = 60+11+14+32 = 117$$
This exactly matches the given $M_{r}$ of 117, so the molecule contains just one empirical unit. The molecular formula is therefore $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{2}$.

Final answer: molecular formula = $\text{C}_{5}\text{H}_{11}\text{NO}_{2}$ because empirical formula mass $= (5 \times 12)+(11 \times 1)+14+(2 \times 16) = 117$ which equals $M_{r}$, so multiplier is 1.
